records.briefDescription: The single true guard of Capo Ferro's system: a low posture with the sword held level in the straight line, point aimed at the adversary's middle, equally prompt to every offense and defense.
records.fullDescription:
Terza is the only guard Capo Ferro recognizes as true. Prima and seconda he does not count as guards at all, and quarta he treats as a way of striking rather than a place of rest. It is a low guard: the sword is held level in a straight line that divides the right flank through the middle, the hilt carried outside the right knee on the right side, neither high nor low. It sits in the middle of the parts that cannot be covered, so that it is equally prompt and near to all offenses and defenses, and the point must always aim at the middle of the adversary's body, on the nearer side.

In lying in terza the head rests on the left shoulder, the body is bent and sloped back with the weight counterpoised over the left leg, and the right arm is somewhat bent so that the sword forms one straight line with the forearm. Its natural strike is the thrust, and it is from terza that the stoccata is sent.
records.briefApplication: Make terza your resting posture and let the thrust be its natural strike; keep the point on the adversary's middle and send the stoccata straight along the line into the nearer side.
records.fullApplication:
From terza you stand equally ready to attack and to defend, because the guard is set in the middle of the parts that cannot be covered and is near to every offense and defense. Hold the point fixed on the middle of the adversary's body, on the nearer side, so that his commitment meets your straight line first and your own strike travels the shortest road.

Prefer terza to the high guards for security. In a high guard your leg can be reached with a thrust or a cut, a danger terza does not carry. Because its natural strike is the thrust, let the stoccata be your answer, sent from terza along the straight line the sword forms with your forearm.

records.briefDescription: The first of the four principal positions, formed with the hilt posted above the shoulder; Capo Ferro counts it a striking posture rather than a true guard, for it uncovers too much of the body.
records.fullDescription:
Prima is the highest of the four principal positions, taken by posting the hilt above the shoulder with the sword arm extended upward. It is the posture into which the weapon naturally falls when first drawn: as you lay hand on the sword and extend the arm, you pass through a high prima before the blade can be settled.

Capo Ferro does not admit prima as a true guard. Together with seconda, it is ill-suited to seeking measure, uncovers too much of the body, and does not stand equally near to all the parts that must be offended and defended, the offices that only the true guard terza fulfills. Prima is therefore treated not as a place of rest but as a means of striking, chiefly the launching posture for the descending thrust.
records.briefApplication: Do not rest in prima; use it as the launching posture for the imbroccata, the descending thrust driven with the false edge from the adversary's left shoulder toward his right knee.
records.fullApplication:
Because prima uncovers too much of the body and is poor for seeking measure, treat it as a moment of striking rather than a station to hold. Its proper blow is the imbroccata: from the high hilt, extend and send the point downward with the false edge, cutting the line from the adversary's left shoulder toward his right knee.

Recognize prima chiefly as the posture into which the sword falls as it is first drawn. Pass through it to deliver the descending thrust, then recover into the true guard terza, where you stand equally ready to offend and defend and can properly seek measure. Do not linger in prima, where the body stands open and the line cannot be safely gained.

records.briefDescription: The position formed when the hilt descends to sit even, or level, with the shoulder; one of the four principal positions, yet a striking posture for offense rather than a true resting guard.
records.fullDescription:
Seconda is one of the four principal positions of the sword, taken when the hilt descends to be even, or level, with the shoulder. From this shoulder-height position the offense is oriented toward the outside line.

For all that it is numbered among the principal positions, Capo Ferro does not count seconda a true guard for resting. Like prima, it is a position from which to strike rather than one in which to wait: it uncovers too much of the body and is not equally near to all the parts, so it cannot answer to every line as terza does. From nature seconda and quarta serve for offense, while terza alone serves for resting in defense.
records.briefApplication: Use seconda to strike on the outside line, as with a thrust to the chest or the face, and to deliver the passata to the face.
records.fullApplication:
Reach for seconda when your work lies on the outside line. The thrust to the chest or to the face on that side is struck in seconda, the hand turned to sit even with the shoulder as the point drives home. It is a position of offense, not a place to settle for defense.

The passata to the face is frequently struck in seconda as well. Yet because the posture uncovers much of the body and is not equally near to all the parts, do not dwell in it: pass through seconda in the very act of striking, and return to terza, the one true resting guard, to answer for your defense.

records.briefDescription: The fourth of the principal positions, formed with the hilt carried inside the thigh; Capo Ferro deems it a way of striking on the inside line rather than a true resting guard.
records.fullDescription:
Quarta is one of the four principal positions of the sword, formed by carrying the hilt across to the inside, held within the line of the left thigh. Turning the hand into quarta opens the inside line and readies the reverse thrust, the punta riversa, which is sent from this position.

Capo Ferro does not number quarta among true guards. He judges that it shows too much of the body and is therefore a way of striking, not of guarding oneself. Paired with terza, it serves as a counter-guard: where terza constrains the adversary's sword on the outside, quarta constrains it on the inside.
records.briefApplication: Turn into quarta to close and constrain the inside line, then loose the punta riversa; when hard-pressed, void the body into the inquartata to strike while carrying yourself offline.
records.fullApplication:
Use quarta whenever the play lies on the inside. Carrying the hilt inside the thigh lets you constrain the adversary's blade on that side, the inside counterpart to stringering in terza on the outside, and from that constraint you deliver the punta riversa straight into the opening.

Because quarta exposes the body, do not rest in it as you would in terza; enter it in the very act of striking or of gaining the inside line, and quit it once the tempo is spent. When the adversary thrusts and you must answer on the inside, deliver the inquartata: strike in quarta while voiding the body, carrying the left leg crossed behind the right so your torso slips from the line as your point arrives.

records.briefDescription: A guard deliberately chosen and posed to oppose and dominate the adversary's guard along a given line of the sword, terza constraining it on the outside and quarta on the inside.
records.fullDescription:
A counter-guard is less a distinct posture than a role any guard assumes when it is chosen and posed specifically to answer the adversary's guard. Its purpose is to oppose and dominate the opposing blade along a given line, so that from the very outset you contest and begin to control his steel rather than merely stand ready before him.

Capo Ferro names terza and quarta as the principal counter-guards: terza serves to constrain, or stringere, the sword on the outside line, while quarta constrains it on the inside line. Yet he holds that all the guards are counter-guards, since each is chosen according to the diversity of the lines of the sword. Forming the correct counter-guard is therefore a matter of reading which line the adversary offers and posing the guard that opposes precisely that line.
records.briefApplication: Read the line your adversary presents, then pose the counter-guard that opposes it: terza to constrain his sword on the outside, quarta to constrain it on the inside. This is how you begin to gain his blade before you seek measure.
records.fullApplication:
Before you close, judge which line of the sword your adversary offers. Against a blade held on the outside, pose terza as your counter-guard and stringere his sword there; against a blade on the inside, pose quarta and constrain it on that line. In each case the counter-guard is chosen to answer his guard, never adopted from mere habit.

The counter-guard is where the encounter begins to be decided. By opposing and dominating his blade along the chosen line, you start to gain his sword before you have closed the distance; only once the correct counter-guard is posed and his steel constrained do you press on to seek measure and strike.

Remember that any guard may serve as a counter-guard when the line demands it. Let the diversity of the lines dictate your choice, so that your posture always opposes his rather than simply mirroring your own preferred stance.

records.briefDescription: The just distance from your sword's point to the adversary's body within which you can strike, and the reckoning by which every action of the sword and of defense is governed.
records.fullDescription:
Measure is the just distance from the point of your sword to the body of your adversary within which you are able to strike him. It is the master reckoning of the art, for all the actions of the sword and of defense take their direction from it; nothing is attempted well until the distance is understood. It is counted in the natural braccio, the length of the arm.

Capo Ferro divides it into two principal measures. Misura larga, wide measure, is the greater distance; misura stretta, narrow measure, is the nearer distance, closer to the adversary's body. The instrument that recognizes measure is the head, held as the sentinel with the eyes ranged along the line of the sword, for by this watch you perceive both measure and tempo at once. To judge and to keep measure well is the ultimate perfection of the guard.
records.briefApplication: Set your eyes along the line of the sword and read the distance in braccia before you commit, striking only when measure and tempo agree. Play the outer game from misura larga, and close to misura stretta, the narrow measure, when you mean to strike.
records.fullApplication:
Before any action, let the head stand as sentinel with the eyes along the line of the sword, for this is what recognizes both measure and tempo together. Judge the just distance in braccia to the adversary's body: are you still outside the distance in which you can strike, or already within it? Let every choice of the sword and of defense be governed by this reckoning rather than by haste.

From misura larga, wide measure, you remain at the greater distance, beyond his immediate reach, where you may make ready before you close. As you come to misura stretta, narrow measure, you stand at the nearer distance, within which you can strike him. Move deliberately between the two and never surrender the distance you have judged, for to keep measure well is the guard's highest perfection and your surest safeguard.

records.briefDescription: The first and outermost of the striking measures, the farthest distance from which you can just reach and strike the adversary, and only by lengthening the pace with an increase of the right foot.
records.fullDescription:
Wide measure is the outermost of the striking measures, the farthest range from which a blow can still land. At this distance the ordinary pace will not carry you home; only by lengthening the pace with an increase of the right foot, the extraordinary pace or long lunge, can the point just arrive on the adversary.

In the reckoning of striking time it corresponds to a tempo and a half. It also serves as a boundary: the act of seeking measure, of closing and gaining the distance, ends at the outer edge of the wide measure, and it is precisely there that the tempo of striking begins.
records.briefApplication: Strike from the outer edge of wide measure by lengthening the pace with the lunge; Capo Ferro prizes this distance because striking from afar is safer and better than striking from nearby.
records.fullApplication:
Treat the outer boundary of wide measure as the threshold where seeking measure ends and striking begins. Close only to this edge, no nearer than you must, and then deliver your blow by lengthening the pace with the increase of the right foot, so the point just reaches home from the greatest distance at which it still can.

Capo Ferro prizes this range because striking from afar is safer and better than striking from nearby: at wide measure you keep the adversary at the very end of your reach while remaining able to hit. Because the blow here costs a tempo and a half, commit the lunge fully, so the extra measure you must cover does not cost you the tempo of striking.

records.briefDescription: The close distance from which you can reach and strike the adversary by driving the body and legs forward over the fixed front foot alone, without any full pass or lunge.
records.fullDescription:
Narrow measure, or misura stretta, is the nearer of the two fencing distances, closer than wide measure. It is defined by what it takes to reach the adversary from it: here you need only push the body and legs forward over the fixed front foot to land your strike, with no full pass and no long lunge required to close the remaining ground.

Because so little distance stands between you and the target, striking from narrow measure demands the fastest and most just tempo, corresponding to a whole tempo. The blow is delivered with the feet fixed, the reach found merely by bending the right knee to carry the body forward onto the point.
records.briefApplication: Strike from narrow measure when wide measure has been lost, whether through your own delay or through the fury of the adversary; keep the feet fixed and merely bend the right knee to reach.
records.fullApplication:
Narrow measure is where an exchange closes, and where you must recover when wide measure has slipped away, whether that loss comes from your own delay or from the fury of an adversary pressing in. When it happens, do not scramble to reset the distance; plant the feet and strike from where you stand, bending only the right knee to reach the mark.

The whole burden of the action falls upon tempo, so guard it jealously. The tempo of narrow measure is lost in two ways: through slowness of nature, when weak or overheavy legs cannot answer in time, and through defect of art, when you approach with the limbs disproportionately spaced. Close correctly instead, carrying the body over the left leg with the right arm extended, so that the moment to strike is never squandered.

records.briefDescription: The very closest of all fencing distances, at which the adversary's committed strike from wide measure leaves his advanced arm exposed to be hit in the fastest possible tempo.
records.fullDescription:
Misura strettissima is the narrowest of all fencing distances, defined not by where you stand at rest but by what it permits. When the adversary launches his attack from misura larga, this is the range at which you can reach his advanced and uncovered arm, whether it carries the sword or the dagger, and strike it as he moves.

Mechanically it belongs to the fastest tempo of all, no more than half a tempo. As the adversary extends, you withdraw the left foot and let the right follow after it, striking his exposed arm in the same instant rather than waiting until his blow has run its course. This is the proper ground of the mezzo tempo, in which the hit lands during the adversary's own action.
records.briefApplication: When the adversary commits a strike from wide measure and leaves his forward arm uncovered, strike that arm during his action, drawing the left foot back and the right after it as you hit.
records.fullApplication:
Reserve misura strettissima for the moment the adversary attacks from misura larga and exposes his advanced arm, be it the sword arm or the dagger arm. Because you are striking in only half a tempo, you do not gather or answer after the fact; you take the arm as it comes forward, catching him in mid-action before his blow can arrive.

The footwork turns a withdrawal into the attack itself: the left foot goes back and the right follows while you strike his exposed arm. Worked well, the mezzo tempo at this measure ends the exchange on his committed arm and denies him the completion of his own attack.

records.briefDescription: Tempo is the measure of motion and stillness in the encounter, the just length of movement or pause needed to reach an end, judged from both fencers together so that one measures the other.
records.fullDescription:
Tempo is the measure of stillness and of motion. Every motion and every stillness, yours and your adversary's alike, together compose a tempo, so that each serves to measure the other. In fencing the word carries three meanings: chiefly the just length of motion or stillness required to reach an end, regardless of how quickly it is made; secondly the quickness of that action relative to how long or short the motion is; and thirdly the striking tempos that arise from measure.

Three striking tempos answer to the three measures. At misura larga, the wide measure, the blow occupies a tempo and a half; at misura stretta, the narrow measure, a whole tempo; and at the very narrowest, half a tempo. The closer you stand, the briefer the tempo in which a blow is completed.

Mechanically, the two speeds of the art are bound to tempo. In the guard and while seeking measure you move slowly, as if shod with a leaden sandal; in the act of striking you move with full speed.
records.briefApplication: Judge tempo from both blades and bodies at once, for the adversary's stillness is a tempo no less than his motion, and never reckon it from his movement alone. Move as if with a leaden sandal while gaining measure, then strike with full speed in the tempo you find.
records.fullApplication:
Read tempo from both combatants together. Capo Ferro warns that many wrongly reckon tempo only from the adversary's movement; in truth his stillness measures your motion as surely as his motion does, and yours measures his. Watch for the moment when his action, or his pause, grants you the just length of time to reach your end.

Fit the striking tempo to the measure you hold. From misura larga expect to strike in a tempo and a half; as you close to misura stretta a whole tempo serves; and at the narrowest, half a tempo is enough to land the point. The nearer the measure, the shorter the window and the less motion you can afford.

Govern your speed accordingly. In guard and while seeking measure, move slowly and deliberately, as if with a leaden sandal; the instant the tempo opens, strike with all quickness.

records.briefDescription: Single time is the act of wounding the adversary with one uninterrupted movement of the sword while at measure, whether narrow or wide, making it the most efficient of all striking actions.
records.fullDescription:
Primo tempo, the first or single time, is reached when you find yourself at measure, be it misura stretta or misura larga, and can strike the adversary with just one movement of the sword. It stands opposed to dui tempi, which requires at least two movements to arrive.

Because a single motion wastes nothing, primo tempo is the most efficient striking action Capo Ferro teaches. Yet he warns of an error common even among masters: disengaging in single time so that one's point arrives upon the enemy's forte, which surrenders the point to the enemy. The sound action does the reverse, carrying your own forte to the enemy's point rather than sending your point onto his forte.
records.briefApplication: Strike in one motion whenever you stand at measure, narrow or wide, choosing single time over two-time actions for its efficiency. When you disengage, always carry your forte to the enemy's point rather than sending your point onto his forte.
records.fullApplication:
When you find yourself at measure, whether misura larga or misura stretta, and an opening lets you reach the adversary with a single movement of the sword, strike in primo tempo. Prefer it to dui tempi, for the single time is the more efficient action and gives the adversary the least room to answer.

Guard against the common fault when you disengage in single time. Do not let a cavazione carry your point onto the enemy's forte, for that gives him the point and leaves your thrust on the weaker leverage. Instead drive your forte against his point, so that your strong opposes his weak as you wound in one tempo.

records.briefDescription: Dui tempi is a striking action that requires at least two separate movements of the sword, such as parrying first and then striking, making it slower and less favored than the single-time primo tempo or the mezzo tempo.
records.fullDescription:
Dui tempi, the two times, is a striking action that demands at least two movements of the sword to complete, the classic example being to parry first and then to strike. Where a single-time answer resolves defense and offense in one motion, dui tempi divides the work into distinct beats.

When you parry in dui tempi, the footwork follows the division of the sword's work: during the tempo of the parry you draw the left foot up to the right, and then pass forward with the right foot as you deliver the strike. Defense and offense thus occupy separate tempi, each with its own movement of blade and body.

Constraining the sword, or stringere, is most often carried out in dui tempi. In the first tempo you acquire the debole of the adversary's sword; in the second you gain the beginning of his forte, closing upon his blade before you come to the strike. Because it spends two movements where one might serve, dui tempi is slower and less preferred than either primo tempo or mezzo tempo.
records.briefApplication: Fall back on dui tempi when you cannot answer in a single time: parry the incoming blade first, then strike. Prefer primo tempo or mezzo tempo wherever the opening allows, since two movements are always slower than one.
records.fullApplication:
Reach for dui tempi when the encounter cannot be settled in a single time and you must first answer the adversary's blade. Parry in two times: during the tempo of the parry draw the left foot up to the right, then pass forward with the right foot as you strike, so that defense and offense fall into their own successive beats.

Use dui tempi as well to constrain the sword. To stringere in two times, acquire the debole of the enemy's blade in the first tempo, then gain the beginning of his forte in the second, dominating his steel before you commit to the strike.

Hold dui tempi as a recourse rather than a first choice. Because two movements take longer than one, it yields the initiative that a faster answer would keep; wherever the tempo permits, prefer the single-time primo tempo or the mezzo tempo, and turn to dui tempi only when the situation forces you to defend before you can offend.

records.briefDescription: Striking in the shortest possible tempo, hitting the adversary's advanced, uncovered arm or catching him the instant he moves, so the blow lands within half a tempo at the narrowest measure.
records.fullDescription:
Mezzo tempo, or half time, is the act of striking within the shortest tempo available to you, corresponding to half a tempo and the narrowest measure. Rather than allowing the adversary to complete a full action, you strike into the smallest opening his movement gives.

Its mechanics differ by distance. At wide measure, misura larga, the target is the adversary's advanced and uncovered arm, whether it carries the sword or the dagger; you reach it with a thrust or a cut before he can bring the rest of his body into play. At narrow measure, misura stretta, you strike him in the very instant he moves to deliver a blow or to perform some other action, taking the tempo his own motion creates.

Redoubling of blows is usually performed in mezzo tempo, one blow following hard upon another within the same short interval.
records.briefApplication: Use mezzo tempo to strike the exposed sword or dagger arm at misura larga, or to hit the adversary the instant he moves at misura stretta; it is also how you redouble your blows.
records.fullApplication:
At wide measure, watch for the advanced, uncovered arm. When the adversary leaves his sword or dagger hand exposed, strike it directly with a thrust or a cut in half a tempo, ending the matter before it becomes a contest of the whole body.

At narrow measure, do not initiate against a settled opponent; instead wait for him to move, whether to strike or to attempt any other action, and drive your blow into that tempo. Because the measure is at its narrowest, the shortest movement of yours suffices to reach him. Use the same half time to redouble, landing a second blow in the interval the first has opened.

Mezzo tempo is Capo Ferro's answer to the bestial man who throws many furious blows without measure or tempo. Do not meet fury with fury; instead strike his sword hand or arm in mezzo tempo during his attack, letting his own reckless motion give you the opening.

records.briefDescription: Counter-time is the act of striking the adversary in the very tempo he moves to attack or to gain your sword, meeting his motion in a shorter tempo and measure so your blow lands first.
records.fullDescription:
Contratempo is a timing action rather than a fixed blow. When the adversary commits a motion to strike you or to gain your sword, that motion is itself a tempo you may seize; instead of waiting or merely parrying, you encounter him and drive your own thrust home in a shorter tempo and a shorter measure, so your point arrives while his action is still forming.

Capo Ferro approves only two forms. In the first, you hold the sword in quarta with the point carried toward your right side; as the adversary moves his right foot to lay his sword upon yours, you push a thrust from quarta while passing forward. In the second, you stand in terza, and as he comes to gain your sword from the outside, you thrust him in seconda while passing. Beyond these, you may also strike beneath his sword in contratempo simply by lowering your body, taking the line under his blade without any parry.
records.briefApplication: Use contratempo the instant the adversary moves to strike or to gain your sword, answering his motion with a thrust in a shorter tempo and measure, whether from quarta or terza while passing, or by dropping your body under his blade.
records.fullApplication:
Reserve contratempo for the moment of the adversary's commitment. When he steps his right foot forward to lay his sword on yours, keep quarta with the point toward your right, then push your thrust from quarta and pass forward, so your point arrives before his engagement is complete. When instead you rest in terza and he comes to gain your sword from the outside, do not follow his blade around; thrust him in seconda and pass, catching him in the very tempo of his gaining.

Where his engagement leaves the low line open, you need not oppose steel at all. Lower your body and strike beneath his sword in contratempo, letting his motion pass over you. In every case the principle holds: his attempt to strike or to gain is the tempo in which you strike, and because you answer in a shorter tempo and measure, your blow lands first.

records.briefDescription: The strong half of the blade, running from the hilt to the middle of the sword, whose office is to parry, to defend, and to dominate the adversary's blade.
records.fullDescription:
The sword divides into two parts, the forte and the debole. The forte, meaning the strong, begins at the hilt and reaches to the middle of the blade. Its office is parrying and defending.

You parry with the forte, from the middle of the sword down to the hilt, opposing the incoming blade with the true edge, and in that meeting you dominate the adversary's sword. Because it serves only to parry and to cover the body, chiefly the head, while you strike, the forte need not even be sharp; its work is strength, not the keenness of its edge.
records.briefApplication: Catch and dominate the adversary's blade on your forte, from the middle of the sword down to the hilt, turning the true edge into the line to parry and cover yourself as you strike.
records.fullApplication:
When you must defend, receive the adversary's blade upon your forte rather than your debole, meeting his steel anywhere from the middle of your sword down to the hilt. Set the true edge against the incoming line so that the strong of your blade dominates his and covers the opening.

Let the forte carry the whole burden of defense while you strike. Cover your body, and above all your head, with the strong of the blade in the same action that delivers your blow, so that one motion both shields and offends. Since the forte answers only for parrying and covering, its sharpness is of no consequence; it is the strength of the strong, met with the true edge, that decides the bind.

records.briefDescription: The debole, or weak, is the forward half of the blade running from its middle to the point, the striking portion of the sword and the only part divided into true and false edges.
records.fullDescription:
The debole, or weak, is the forward half of the sword, reaching from the middle of the blade to the point. It is the striking half, the part that carries a thrust home and delivers a cut.

Capo Ferro divides the debole alone into a true edge and a false edge, a distinction he never draws in the forte. When you cut, the blow is made with the debole, slicing along its sharpest part.
records.briefApplication: Reserve the debole for striking, thrusting home or cutting with its keenest part; when you constrain the sword through stringere, acquire the enemy's debole with a palmo, a hand's breadth, of your own.
records.fullApplication:
Reserve the debole for offense. It is the part that reaches the adversary, so thrusts finish with it and cuts land with its sharpest section, slicing rather than merely striking. Because it alone bears both true and false edge, it is the half that carries your cutting work.

When you close and constrain the enemy's blade through stringere, gain his debole with a palmo, a hand's breadth, of your own debole. Commanding his weak half with a controlled span of yours governs his sword.

records.briefDescription: The true edge is the edge that faces downward when the hand rests in its natural position, as in terza, and it is Capo Ferro's preferred edge for parrying because it turns more quickly.
records.fullDescription:
The filo dritto is the true edge of the blade, the edge that faces downward when the hand rests in its natural position, as it does in the guard of terza. It is the edge you defend with by default.

In Capo Ferro's division of the blade, only the debole is spoken of as having a true and a false edge, so this is where the distinction of edge is drawn. When you parry with the true edge, however, you do so with the forte, meeting the adversary's blade with the strong of your sword from the middle down to the hilt, and the parry may travel in either a straight or an oblique line.
records.briefApplication: Parry with the true edge for greater safety, since it turns more quickly than the false edge; take the incoming blade on your forte, from the middle of the sword down to the hilt.
records.fullApplication:
From terza, let the true edge be your natural means of defense. Capo Ferro advises parrying with it rather than the false edge for greater safety, since the true edge turns more quickly and brings your defense into place with less delay.

Take the adversary's blade on your forte, from the middle of your sword down to the hilt, where the strong of the blade opposes his steel most firmly, and let the parry run in a straight or an oblique line as the angle of the attack demands. It is the combination of the forte's strength and the quicker turn of the true edge that makes this the safer parry.

records.briefDescription: The back edge of the rapier, opposite the true edge, brought to bear when the hand turns outward or inward from its natural orientation, and named either falso dritto or falso manco.
records.fullDescription:
The false edge is the edge of the rapier opposite the true edge, engaged when the hand turns out of, or inward from, its natural orientation. It takes two names according to the way the hand rolls: the falso dritto, which carries the edge toward the enemy's right side, and the falso manco, which carries it toward his left.

Mechanically the false edge does several kinds of work. It beats the adversary's blade aside, driving his sword to his right with the falso dritto and to his left with the falso manco. When it parries, the parry is taken from the middle of the sword up to the point. It also shapes certain thrusts: the imbroccata is thrown with the false edge turned downward, and in low quarta the sword is covered by setting the debole, the false edge, over the enemy's point.
records.briefApplication: Beat the enemy's sword to his right with the falso dritto and to his left with the falso manco; from the falso manco follow with either a thrust or a cut.
records.fullApplication:
Use the falso dritto to beat the enemy's sword toward his right side, and the falso manco to beat it toward his left. From the falso manco, once his blade is displaced, you may strike with either a thrust or a cut.

When you must defend with the false edge, parry along the portion from the middle of the sword up to the point. To attack downward, throw the imbroccata with the false edge turned down. And when you stand in low quarta, cover the enemy's point by laying your debole, the false edge, over it.

records.briefDescription: To constrain the sword is to gain it: engaging the adversary's blade in the straight line, your forte set over his debole, so as to close measure and uncover an opening to strike.
records.fullDescription:
To stringer the sword means as much as to gain it: to constrain the adversary's blade so that you may come to measure and uncover him, whether outside or inside, high or low, and whether he stands fixed or moves. It is always performed in the straight line, and Capo Ferro cautions that you should constrain only when you cannot do otherwise.

Mechanically, you engage the debole of the enemy's sword with your forte in a straight line, straddling his blade without touching it, and touching and striking his debole only in the very act of striking. It is most often done in dui tempi: first acquire his debole with a palmo of your own debole, then acquire the beginning of his forte. Throughout, your forte must always accompany your debole, and the whole gaining must move together with the motion of the leg.

The line of the constraint is chosen by your posture: terza constrains on the outside, quarta constrains on the inside.
records.briefApplication: Constrain only when you cannot come to measure and uncover the adversary by any other means. From terza gain the outside line, from quarta the inside, straddling his debole with your forte as you close.
records.fullApplication:
Use stringere to bring yourself to measure and lay bare an opening, but reserve it for when no simpler path uncovers the adversary, constraining only when you cannot do otherwise. Read the line first: from terza take the outside, from quarta take the inside, uncovering him high or low as the opening presents, and gain the same way whether his sword is fixed or moving.

Work it in dui tempi. In the first time acquire his debole with a palmo of your own debole; in the second, press on to acquire the beginning of his forte, keeping your point in the straight line so that the constraint itself already threatens him. Let your forte always accompany your debole, and unite the gaining of the blade with the motion of your leg, so that closing his sword and closing the measure become a single action.

Straddle his blade without touching it, holding your line clean, and let the touch come only when you strike his debole. Constrain, close, and uncover in one continuous approach, so that the moment the line is gained you are already in measure to deliver the thrust.

records.briefDescription: The act of achieving domination over the adversary's blade from any guard, which Capo Ferro holds to be one and the same as stringere, constraining the sword.
records.fullDescription:
To gain the sword is to acquire mastery of the adversary's blade out of any of the guards, and Capo Ferro treats it as identical to stringere, the constraining of the sword. It is held in two manners. In the first, you have acquired the adversary's sword and never quit that domination even while you strike. In the second, you have beaten his sword out of your presence and strike before it can recover.

Mechanically you constrain the blade about one palmo from its point. Constraining on the inside, you aim your own point at his right shoulder; constraining on the outside, you aim it at his left shoulder. Having thus set your point against him, you walk in while keeping the domination unbroken.
records.briefApplication: Constrain the adversary's blade about a palmo from its point, aiming your point at his right shoulder on the inside or his left on the outside, then walk in without ever surrendering the domination you have won.
records.fullApplication:
Gain before you advance: do not come in to strike until you have first dominated his blade. In the first manner, hold the constraint through the whole action so your thrust arrives while his steel is still bound and cannot answer. In the second, when you have beaten his blade out of your presence, drive home at once, before it recovers.

Should the adversary instead gain your sword, never disengage in order to throw a completed blow. Recover your blade by ceding the body and lowering the sword, and as he presses forward to gain it anew, strike him in that very approach.

records.briefDescription: The cavazione carries your point under or over the adversary's blade into the opposite line, freeing your sword to gain or quit measure in tempo, forward or back, and to answer being constrained.
records.fullDescription:
The cavazione, or disengage, carries the point from one line to the other, passing it under or over the opposing blade. It is performed in tempo, whether stepping forward or back, to exit a bind or to acquire measure. Its principal office is as the answer to constraint: when the adversary has gained your sword by stringere and drawn it off the straight line, you cede a little with the body or the feet, disengage, and immediately replace yourself in the straight line so your point again threatens.

The two forms differ in mechanics. Disengaging under, done in order to constrain him in turn, is made with the arm extended and a small increase of the foot, so the point slips beneath his blade to the other line. Disengaging over is made with a ceding of the body: carry the sword in an oblique line to the rear until its point clears the adversary's point, then replace your forte above his.
records.briefApplication: Use the cavazione the instant the adversary gains your blade and carries it from the straight line: cede a little, disengage under or over, and reclaim the line so your point again threatens. Do not disengage out of habit, for repeated disengages only squander tempo.
records.fullApplication:
Reach for the disengage when you are constrained. When the adversary has gained your sword by stringere and pushed it off the straight line, do not oppose strength to strength; cede a little with the body or the feet, disengage to the free line, and replace yourself at once in the straight line so your point recovers its threat. Choose disengaging under, arm extended with a small increase of the foot, when you mean to constrain him in your turn; choose disengaging over, ceding the body and carrying the point obliquely to the rear to clear his point, when you wish to set your forte above his.

The cavazione also governs measure. Because it is done in tempo, you may use it to exit measure or to acquire it, moving forward or back as the moment demands.

Temper its use. Capo Ferro condemns habitual feints, disengages, and counter-disengages as vanities that lose tempo, so never disengage for its own sake. A single feinted disengage, made while holding the body back, may bait a confident adversary into committing to a counter you can then exploit.

records.briefDescription: The counter-disengage is a second, answering disengage that follows the adversary's cavazione, returning your blade to the line and place it held so his change of line fails against your constraint.
records.fullDescription:
The contracavazione is the answer to the adversary's disengage. Having constrained his sword, you find that he attempts to escape by carrying his point to the other side; the counter-disengage follows that motion and returns your own sword to its previous line and place, so that the constraint you had established is restored rather than broken.

Mechanically it is formed as a single, unbroken turn of the blade that traces the adversary's cavazione and comes back to where it began. Throughout the action your forte must always accompany your debole in a straight line, and this motion of the sword travels together with the motion of the leg, so that hand and body move as one and the point is never lost from the line.

Because it merely returns the sword to its place, the contracavazione may be completed as a pure recovery of the constraint, or, in the very tempo of his disengage, it may carry through as a strike delivered along the same line.
records.briefApplication: Use the contracavazione the instant you have gained the sword and the adversary disengages to escape it; follow his blade back to its old line, or, in that same tempo, drive your point home.
records.fullApplication:
From a constrained sword, watch for the adversary's disengage: he cannot free himself while you hold his blade, so he will attempt to change lines against your constraint. In that same instant answer with the contracavazione, following his blade around and setting your sword back into the line and place it occupied. His attempt to change lines is thereby defeated and he gains nothing by the exchange.

You have two ends from this one action. You may counter-disengage simply to recover your constraint, remaining master of his sword and ready to strike on the next tempo. Or, with that same counter-disengage, you may strike him in the very tempo of his disengage, letting the return of your blade carry your point into him as he opens the line.

In either case keep your forte accompanying your debole in a straight line and let the sword move together with the leg, for it is this union of blade and body that lets the counter-disengage both close the line he sought to open and, when you choose, deliver the thrust in the same motion.

records.briefDescription: A deceitful gesture of the sword, cut or thrust, that threatens one line and strikes at the opposite, which Capo Ferro condemns in theory yet demonstrates in practice.
records.fullDescription:
A finta is a deceitful gesture of the sword, made of the cut or the thrust, that threatens one line while striking at the opposite. It can be offered outside or inside, high or low, straight or circular, so that the adversary answers the false menace and leaves open the true one. Against a feint one may in turn answer with a counter-feint, the deception set against the deception.

In his book on the art Capo Ferro condemns feints as vanities that lose tempo and measure. He gives a plain rule: if the feint is made out of measure, do not move, for it costs the adversary his tempo and gains him nothing; if it is made in measure, strike during it, taking your blow in the very tempo he wastes on the gesture.

Yet in the use he demonstrates the feinted disengage. Disengage as a feint while holding the body back somewhat, so the menace looks committed but your person remains withdrawn and safe. The confident adversary, drawn in by the apparent opening, launches his own committed attack, which you then parry and answer with your counter.
records.briefApplication: Do not move against a feint made out of measure; strike into one made in measure, and use the feinted disengage to draw a confident adversary onto your parry and counter.
records.fullApplication:
Judge the feint by the measure, exactly as Capo Ferro instructs. When the adversary offers a feint out of measure, do not move: his gesture threatens one line and reaches nothing, and by staying still you spend no tempo and give him no opening to strike into. When he feints in measure, do not answer the false menace but strike during it, taking your thrust in the tempo he loses on the deceit. In this way his own vanity delivers him to your point.

When you are the one deceiving, use the feinted disengage. Disengage as a feint but keep the body drawn back somewhat, so that your menace looks like a true commitment while your person stays out of danger. The confident adversary reads the opening as real and commits his attack; because you never truly extended, you remain composed to parry his blade and return your counter into the line he has abandoned.

Set a counter-feint against an adversary who fences by feints, meeting his deception with your own. But hold to the master's warning: treat the feint as a thing to punish or exploit rather than to lean upon, for in the art it loses tempo and measure, and only in the disciplined use of the feinted disengage does it serve you.

records.briefDescription: A feint performed from low quarta in which you cover the point of the adversary's sword with your debole along the straight line, neutralizing his threatening point while you prepare to strike.
records.fullDescription:
Coprire la spada is a kind of feint. From low quarta, you cover the point of the adversary's sword with the debole of your own blade, and this must always be done in a straight line.

By covering his point in this way you neutralize the threat it poses, taking control of the dangerous end of his weapon while you make ready to strike. The action is a preparation rather than an attack in itself: it is the deception worked upon the adversary that opens the way for the blow to follow.

Do not confuse it with stringere, or constraining. In stringere you engage the enemy's debole with your forte in the straight line in order to gain his blade outright; in covering you instead lay your debole over his point from low quarta, deceiving him rather than seizing the sword.
records.briefApplication: Use it from low quarta when the adversary threatens you with his point: cover that point with your debole in the straight line to neutralize the threat, then strike while he is deceived.
records.fullApplication:
When the adversary presents a threatening point, come to low quarta and cover his point with your debole, keeping strictly to the straight line. Once his point is covered it can no longer menace you, and the covering itself acts as a feint that fixes his attention while you prepare.

Having neutralized his point, use the moment you have won to make ready and deliver your strike. Because covering is a feint and not a true gaining of the blade, do not rely on it to hold his sword as stringere would; treat it as the preparation that clears the line and deceives him, then strike into the opening it creates.

Keep clear in your mind the difference from stringere. If your aim is to command his blade with your forte and gain it, constrain; if your aim is to deceive him and cover his point with your debole from low quarta, cover the sword. Choose according to whether you mean to seize the blade or to feint past it.

records.briefDescription: A cut delivered from the right side; in its ordinary form it falls on an oblique line from the adversary's left shoulder to his right knee, and it takes several forms.
records.fullDescription:
The mandritto is the cut that begins from the right side. In its ordinary form it crosses on an oblique line, descending from the enemy's left shoulder to his right knee. Beyond this ordinary cut it takes several forms: the fendente, the tondo, the montante, the stramazzone and the ridoppio.

Like the riverso, the mandritto is driven by the motion of the elbow; when the measure and the tempo allow, it is thrown with the whole arm. The blow lands by slicing, cutting with the debole, the weak of the blade nearest the point.
records.briefApplication: Keep the mandritto out of narrow measure, where cutting uncovers the body and the thrust is surer. Save it for when a cut serves better than a point, favoring the descending forms and slicing with the debole.
records.fullApplication:
Capo Ferro holds the thrust superior to the cut at narrow measure, because to cut is to uncover the body and give an opening in the very act of striking. Treat the mandritto accordingly: do not reach for it in misura stretta, where the point is surer, but keep it for the moments and distances where a cut serves better than a thrust.

Favor the descending forms, for these retain their use even in a thrust-centered system. Drive the cut from the elbow when you must be quick and contained, and open into the whole arm only when the measure and tempo give you room to commit. Strike by slicing with the debole rather than chopping, so the edge does its work as the blade passes.

records.briefDescription: The cut delivered from the left, or reversed, side of the body, made with the motion of the elbow or the whole arm, and taking the same forms as its counterpart the mandritto.
records.fullDescription:
The riverso is the cut thrown from the left, the reversed side, mirroring the mandritto that falls from the right. Like the mandritto it is not one blow but a family of blows: it comes in ordinary, fendente, tondo, montante, stramazzone and ridoppio forms, so a riverso may descend, sweep across, rise, or double back upon its own line as the moment demands.

Mechanically it is driven by the motion of the elbow when time is short, or by the whole arm when measure and tempo allow a fuller, more committed cut. Because it opens from the left, its natural targets are the adversary's exposed openings, chiefly the arm or the face.
records.briefApplication: Cut at the exposed arm or face rather than the leg, and favor a riverso to the face as you withdraw into terza to close the action safely.
records.fullApplication:
Choose your target with care. A riverso to the leg is dangerous to the one who throws it, for reaching the low line leans the body too far forward and loses your measure, leaving you exposed. The shrewd fencer refuses this bait and strikes instead at the exposed arm or the face, targets that lie nearer and demand no such over-commitment.

A dependable finish is the riverso to the face delivered as you withdraw, gathering yourself back into terza as the cut lands. This lets you wound the upper opening while recovering both posture and distance in one motion, ending the exchange covered rather than committed.

records.briefDescription: A descending cut that falls in a straight line from high to low, delivered as either a mandritto or a riverso, and more vigorous than cuts checked short above the waist.
records.fullDescription:
The fendente is the cleaving cut, travelling in a straight line from high to low, top to bottom. It comes in two forms: the mandritto fendente, falling from the right, and the riverso fendente, falling from the left.

Mechanically it is a descending blow that strikes with the debole, the weak of the blade, drawing through the target as a slice rather than arresting the edge. Because it continues its fall rather than stopping above the waist, it carries more vigor than cuts checked short, committing the edge fully down the line of the strike.
records.briefApplication: Deliver the fendente when you want a vigorous descending cut that carries fully through the target, and chain a mandritto fendente to the head after a riverso to the face for a safer combination.
records.fullApplication:
Throw the fendente as a committed descending blow, letting the debole slice down the straight line from high to low rather than halting the edge above the waist, which would rob the cut of its force.

Use the two forms in concert. Lead with a riverso to the face, and let a mandritto fendente to the head follow as the safer combination. Favor the fuller descending path over a shortened one, since the cut that falls all the way through strikes with the greater vigor.

records.briefDescription: A horizontal cut turning crosswise from the right, sweeping the blade along a flat arc rather than descending or rising, the mandritto form of the tondo or round cut.
records.fullDescription:
The tondo, or round cut, is the blow that turns crosswise along a horizontal arc, distinct from the descending fendente and the rising montante. In its mandritto form it travels from the right side across the adversary, sweeping level rather than falling or climbing.

It is delivered with the motion of the elbow alone when space is tight, opening the arc to the whole arm when the measure and tempo permit a fuller sweep. The mandritto tondo is one of the two round cuts, the other being its mirror, the riverso tondo.
records.briefApplication: Use the mandritto tondo to strike crosswise from the right along a horizontal line; keep it to the elbow in close, and open it to the whole arm when measure and tempo allow.
records.fullApplication:
Reach for the mandritto tondo when the horizontal line is the one left open, where a fendente or montante would not arrive cleanly. Because it turns crosswise, it sweeps across the adversary from your right, and you govern its extent by how much arm you commit.

In close, drive it with the elbow so the blow stays compact and quick. When the measure widens and the tempo is yours, extend the motion to the whole arm for a fuller round cut. Pair it in thought with its mirror, the riverso tondo, so that whichever crosswise line opens, right or left, you have the round cut to answer it.

records.briefDescription: A rising cut delivered with the true edge from below, ascending along a vertical line to strike the point of the adversary's right shoulder, and formed as a variant of both the mandritto and the riverso.
records.fullDescription:
The montante is a cut that ascends rather than falls. It departs with the true edge from below and rises along a vertical line to strike the point of the adversary's right shoulder, making it the direct opposite of the descending fendente, which comes down from above.

Because its defining trait is this rising vertical path taken with the true edge, the montante is not a blow apart but a form that either the mandritto or the riverso can assume. Whether it travels as a mandritto or as a riverso, the montante keeps the same upward line and the same target at the shoulder's point.
records.briefApplication: Use the montante when the blow you intend must climb from below to the adversary's right shoulder, choosing it as the rising true-edge form of either your mandritto or your riverso.
records.fullApplication:
When an opening appears at the point of the adversary's right shoulder, answer it with the montante, driving the true edge upward along its vertical rising line to strike that mark. Because the montante rises where the fendente falls, reach for it whenever the cut you mean to deliver must ascend from below to its target rather than descend upon it.

Treat the montante as the rising expression of your mandritto and riverso rather than a separate technique. When the cut you intend must climb to reach the right shoulder, give it the upward line of the montante; when it must instead come down, give it the fendente.

records.briefDescription: A quick circular wrist-cut delivered in the manner of a turning wheel, standing as one of the cut-forms of both the mandritto and the riverso.
records.fullDescription:
The stramazzone is a cut thrown in the manner of a wheel: a compact, circular blow driven almost entirely from the wrist rather than the arm or shoulder. Its defining quality is speed and economy, the blade wheeling over in a tight rotation so the edge arrives without the wide committal of a full descending cut.

Because it is a form of delivery rather than a separate line, the stramazzone can be given as either a mandritto or a riverso, taking its name and side from the direction in which the wrist turns the edge. It is the wheeling expression of those cuts, a means of striking with a small, rapid circle of the point and edge.
records.briefApplication: Use the stramazzone as a fast wrist-cut to the arm, especially to counter an adversary who overcommits, catching the exposed limb without the exposure of a larger blow.
records.fullApplication:
Reach for the stramazzone when you want to strike the arm quickly and take advantage of a fault in your opponent's turn. Capo Ferro shows it thrown to the arm as a counter against an adversary who leans too far forward while turning a riverso: as he overextends and carries his body past his defense, wheel your wrist over and cut his exposed arm.

The value of the blow here is its economy. Because it turns from the wrist as a tight wheel rather than a full swing, you can answer his committed action in the moment it opens him, striking the arm without abandoning your own line or opening yourself to his recovery.

records.briefDescription: A two-part cutting action in which a half mandritto beats down the adversary's sword and is followed at once by a full mandritto to strike, and which works equally on the reversed side.
records.fullDescription:
The ridoppio, or redoubling, is a compound cutting action built from two blows delivered on the same side. You begin with a mezzo mandritto, a half cut that knocks down the adversary's sword and clears his line, then return to him at once with a second, ordinary mandritto that delivers the true blow.

The action mirrors on the reversed side, opening with a mezzo riverso to beat the blade aside and following with a full riverso. Because it doubles a strike within one continuous motion, redoubling is generally performed in mezzo tempo, the half time, so the second cut follows the first before the adversary can recover his sword or answer.
records.briefApplication: Use the ridoppio when a half cut has knocked the opponent's sword aside; redouble immediately with a full mandritto, or a full riverso on the other side, landing in mezzo tempo before he recovers.
records.fullApplication:
Throw a mezzo mandritto to strike down the adversary's blade and command his line. The moment his sword is beaten aside, do not withdraw or reset; redouble at once with a full mandritto into the opening you have made, landing the true blow while his weapon is still displaced.

Perform the redoubling in mezzo tempo, the half time, so that the second cut arrives before he can lift his sword back into line or reply. Work the same pattern on the reversed side, leading with a mezzo riverso to knock the sword down and following with a full riverso. Because both blows fall on one side in a single flowing action, the ridoppio turns a beat on the blade into a hit rather than leaving you at a mere parry.

records.briefDescription: A strike or beat delivered with the false edge, made in two manners: the falso dritto against the adversary's sword toward his right, and the falso manco toward his left.
records.fullDescription:
The falso is a strike or beat performed not with the true edge but with the false edge of the blade. Capo Ferro designates it in two manners according to the direction of its action. The falso dritto is directed to hit the enemy's sword toward his right side, while the falso manco is directed toward his left.

Mechanically, the two forms differ in what they permit afterward. The falso dritto serves to displace or beat the opposing blade to the right. The falso manco is the more versatile of the pair, for from it you may continue with either a thrust or a cut. Note well that the falso is a means of beating and striking, not of defending: when the purpose is to parry, turning the wrist to receive the blade on the true edge is both safer and quicker than parrying with the false edge.
records.briefApplication: Beat the adversary's sword aside with the falso dritto toward his right or the falso manco toward his left, and follow the falso manco with either a thrust or a cut as the opening allows.
records.fullApplication:
Use the falso to act upon the enemy's blade rather than to guard against it. Employ the falso dritto to drive his sword toward his right side, and the falso manco to drive it toward his left. When you choose the falso manco, keep both options alive, for from it you may finish with a thrust or with a cut according to how the opening presents itself.

Falsing under the enemy's sword is especially fruitful, for it sets up the voids and prepares the inquartata, carrying your body offline as your blade works beneath his. Reserve the falso for these offensive and provoking actions. When you must truly parry, do not trust the false edge; turn the wrist and take his blade on the true edge instead, which is the safer and quicker defense.

records.briefDescription: The stoccata is the thrust sent from the guard of terza toward the adversary's right shoulder, and it stands as the natural strike of Capo Ferro's system, more mortal than the cut and keeping the sword in presence.
records.fullDescription:
The stoccata is the thrust thrown from the guard of terza, sent to strike the adversary toward his right shoulder. It is the natural strike of the system: from terza, only the throwing of the thrust counts as the natural blow, so this thrust is the direct expression of the guard itself rather than a departure from it.

Capo Ferro exhorts the fencer always to strike with the thrust. He holds it superior to the cut for two reasons: it is more mortal, and it does not remove the sword from presence. Where a cut swings the blade away and leaves you open in the withdrawal, the stoccata keeps the point fixed on the adversary throughout the action, so your threat is never surrendered.
records.briefApplication: Strike with the stoccata from terza whenever you can, since the thrust is more mortal than the cut and never removes your point from presence; against an uncovered arm, deliver it to the advanced hand in mezzo tempo.
records.fullApplication:
Make the stoccata your default answer from terza. Because it is the natural strike of the guard, you do not need to reshape your posture to deliver it; you simply drive the point from terza toward the adversary's right shoulder. Prefer it to the cut on principle: it is more mortal, and it keeps your sword in presence so that even an unsuccessful attempt continues to menace him rather than exposing you.

Against an uncovered arm, use the stoccata to the advanced hand, delivered in mezzo tempo. When the adversary carries his forward hand unguarded, this thrust reaches the nearest and most exposed target in a half-time, punishing the opening before he can close it while your point never leaves the line.

records.briefDescription: A high descending thrust launched from the guard of prima, driving from the adversary's left shoulder down toward his right knee with the false edge turned downward.
records.fullDescription:
The imbroccata is the descending thrust, sent from the guard of prima. Its line runs high and falls downward, striking from the adversary's left shoulder toward his right knee, and it is carried with the false edge turned downward.

Mechanically it is delivered over the arm or over the sword, a thrust that comes down from above rather than up from below. The hand is held in prima and is not turned as the thrust is delivered; only as the point of the attack arrives and needs to fall does the hand turn, seating the thrust downward into its mark.
records.briefApplication: Loose the imbroccata over the arm or sword to strike along the high, descending line, and use it as a counter to the chest once you have parried the adversary's blade to the outside.
records.fullApplication:
From the guard of prima, send the imbroccata when the high line lies open, driving from the adversary's left shoulder down toward his right knee. Keep the hand in prima as the thrust travels and turn it only as the point arrives and must fall, so the thrust drops downward and seats into the mark.

The imbroccata serves especially well as a counter. When you have parried to the outside and cleared the adversary's high line, answer with an imbroccata to the chest, carried over his arm or sword, letting the descending line bring your point home before he can recover.

records.briefDescription: One of Capo Ferro's three named thrusts, sent from the guard of quarta to strike outside the adversary's shoulder with the hand well reversed to the inside, rising from low toward the breast.
records.fullDescription:
The punta riversa, or reverse thrust, is delivered from the guard of quarta and takes its name from the reversed hand that shapes it. As you extend, the hand turns well over to the inside, carrying the blade across and outside the enemy's shoulder.

When your sword rests in a low guard, the punta riversa rises from below, climbing upward along a line that ends at the adversary's breast. It stands with the stoccata and the imbroccata as one of the three named thrusts of the system, distinguished from them by its origin in quarta and by the strong inward reversal of the hand.
records.briefApplication: Use the punta riversa when the opening lies outside the adversary's shoulder: turn the hand well over to the inside and drive the point up from your low guard toward the breast.
records.fullApplication:
From a low guard, answer an opening outside the shoulder by rolling the hand into quarta and sending the point up and across into the breast. The strong inward reversal of the hand carries your blade outside the adversary's shoulder as you commit.

Hold the punta riversa among your three thrusts as the reply to the outside quarter. Where the stoccata and the imbroccata find their own lines, this thrust takes the one that climbs from below and passes outside the shoulder. Choose it when the adversary leaves that quarter open and you can reach the breast from your low guard.

records.briefDescription: Capo Ferro's signature extended thrust, delivered at misura larga by driving the whole body and rear leg forward as the sword arm extends, reaching the farthest and safest striking distance in one tempo.
records.fullDescription:
The botta lunga is Capo Ferro's signature extended thrust, the long blow whose reach comes from the whole body committing to the strike. It is delivered at wide measure with an extraordinary pace in which every member is moved to strike at once, closing distance that a merely outstretched arm never could.

Mechanically, the left leg drives the body and the right leg forward while the right arm extends the sword. The left leg extends as a slope, and the right leg forms a pillar and buttress that bears the weight of the body. Because the measure is increased by the extension of the body and the forward pace, and not merely by extending the arm, all the members move together in one tempo to reach the farthest and safest striking distance.
records.briefApplication: Use the botta lunga to strike from misura larga, launching the thrust in a single tempo so the whole body carries the point to a target your adversary believes to be beyond reach.
records.fullApplication:
From terza, when you stand at misura larga and an opening shows, deliver the botta lunga as one committed action. The left leg drives the body and the right leg forward, the right leg forming a pillar and buttress that bears your weight, while the right arm extends the sword so that every member reaches the target in the same instant.

Because the measure is gained by the extension of the body and the forward pace, not by the arm alone, you can reach an adversary who believes himself safe, arriving at the farthest and safest striking distance. Loose it in a single tempo, all the members moving together, so the thrust lands as one motion rather than a preparation your adversary can answer.

records.briefDescription: The natural, comfortable footing—counterpoised over the left leg—in which one rests in guard and seeks the narrow measure little by little, judged by Capo Ferro the best pace of all.
records.fullDescription:
The ordinary pace, which Capo Ferro also names the military or soldierly pace, is the natural and comfortable footing of the fencer. The body is counterpoised over the left leg, and it is in this pace that one rests in guard and seeks the narrow measure.

Capo Ferro judges it the best pace of all. Any smaller pace draws the feet too close together, making the base narrow and weak, no longer able to support the body. The ordinary pace keeps the base broad enough to hold you strong and steady, and from it measure is gained little by little rather than by hurried steps and half-paces that would lose the tempo.
records.briefApplication: Rest in the ordinary pace whenever you stand in guard, and from it seek the narrow measure little by little—never with hurried steps or half-paces, which lose the tempo.
records.fullApplication:
From the ordinary pace, hold your weight counterpoised over the left leg and rest in guard. Take this as your working footing: it is the best pace of all, broad enough to support the body securely, whereas any smaller pace narrows the base and leaves it too weak to hold you.

Use this pace to seek the narrow measure. Close little by little; do not gain ground with hurried steps and half-paces, for such haste loses the tempo. Advance gradually and stay counterpoised over the left leg, so that you arrive at misura stretta still balanced, still in guard, and ready to strike or defend.

records.briefDescription: The lengthened forward pace of the botta lunga, in which the right knee bends fully to its most acute angle while the left leg extends forward as a slope, reaching to strike at wide measure.
records.fullDescription:
The extraordinary pace is the pace into which you move by lengthening your step forward in order to strike; it is the pace of the lunge, the botta lunga. It is not a resting position but a committed reaching action that carries the body and the point to the adversary in one motion.

Mechanically, as you strike the right knee bends fully to form the most acute angle, seating your weight over the forward foot, while the left leg extends forward as a slope, driving the body along the line of the thrust. The reach of this increased, extraordinary foot is what defines wide measure: the outer edge of the distance from which the lunge can touch.

Having struck with the extraordinary pace, right foot forward, you do not remain extended. You recover by retiring back into an ordinary pace and returning into guard.
records.briefApplication: Use the extraordinary pace to deliver the botta lunga from misura larga, lengthening the forward step so the point and the body arrive together; the instant the blow lands, retire and recover.
records.fullApplication:
From terza at wide measure, the extraordinary pace is your instrument for closing and striking in a single lengthening of the step. Extend the forward pace into the botta lunga so that the thrust arrives as the body arrives, the right knee bent to its most acute angle and the left leg extended forward as a slope to carry your weight into the point.

Let this pace govern your sense of distance. Because wide measure is defined precisely by the reach of the increased, extraordinary foot, the extraordinary pace tells you the exact remove from which a full lunge can touch. Strike from within that reach, and do not commit the lunge from any farther.

Do not dwell in the extended position once you have struck. Having landed with the right foot forward, recover at once by retiring into an ordinary pace and settling back into guard, ready to renew the attack or to defend.

records.briefDescription: The increase of pace is the lengthening of the step, driving the forward foot ahead to gain reach and close distance so that a blow can arrive on the adversary.
records.fullDescription:
The accrescimento is a lengthening of the pace, driving the forward foot ahead to extend the reach and carry the body toward the adversary in order to reach and strike. It is the means by which wide measure, misura larga, is attained: that distance is gained with the increase of the right foot.

How much the pace increases is governed by the depth of the narrow measure that must be crossed. When striking, you either keep fixed feet or add the increase of the pace according to the size of that narrow measure, lengthening the step only as far as the ground before you demands. A slight constraint calls for only a small increase of the foot, as when you disengage beneath the adversary's blade to constrain his sword.
records.briefApplication: Increase the pace to reach the adversary while he is still seeking measure, gaining misura larga with the right foot; but when he moves to strike, hold to fixed feet rather than lengthening your step.
records.fullApplication:
Use the accrescimento to reach. When the adversary stands at wide measure, gain misura larga with the increase of the right foot so that your point can arrive; let the depth of the narrow measure that remains decide whether you add pace or strike from where you stand.

Above all, time the increase against his own motion. Strike him with the increase of pace while he is still seeking measure, for then the added reach closes the ground he has not yet covered and your blow lands before he is set. But when he commits and moves to strike, do not lengthen your step: strike with fixed feet, keeping your base beneath you rather than reaching your body into his blow.

When you disengage under his blade to constrain the sword and press toward stringere, accompany the action with only a small increase of the foot, enough to close and constrain without overextending your base.

records.briefDescription: A passing step in which the rear left leg advances past the front leg to close distance, which Capo Ferro condemns in theory for losing measure and tempo yet employs in certain closing attacks.
records.fullDescription:
The passata, or passing step, is a footwork action in which the rear left leg travels forward and passes the front right leg, exchanging the lead so that the whole body advances rather than merely extending over the front foot.

In his treatment of the art, Capo Ferro condemns the passata as an action that loses both measure and tempo. His reasoning is mechanical: while the left leg is in motion, the torso, the right leg, and the sword arm cannot move to strike with due speed, leaving the fencer unable to deliver cleanly and exposed to a response from the adversary.

In the use, however, he still demonstrates passing attacks. He shows a strike to the face delivered in seconda upon a passata while giving a grip to the enemy's sword hand, and he delivers the scannatura with a passata of the left leg.
records.briefApplication: Avoid the passata as an ordinary means of striking, since it surrenders measure and tempo; reserve it for committed closing actions, such as a thrust to the face in seconda while gripping the enemy's sword hand, or to deliver the scannatura.
records.fullApplication:
Treat the passata as an exception rather than a habit. Because the passing left leg carries your torso, right leg, and sword arm out of striking readiness, using it to reach the adversary costs you speed and invites his counter; for ordinary offense, keep to actions in which the sword and body strike together in one tempo.

When you do pass, commit fully to closing and controlling. Strike the face in seconda as you pass, and in the same action lay a grip upon the enemy's sword hand, so that while you occupy his weapon he cannot answer your entry.

Reserve the passata likewise for the scannatura, driven home with a passata of the left leg. Use it only once you have earned the moment to close, never as a substitute for striking in place from the line.

records.briefDescription: A voiding of the body that evades the adversary's line of attack by carrying the torso or a leg clear of it, used in place of a parry or together with one.
records.fullDescription:
The scanso is defensive footwork of the whole body: instead of meeting the incoming blade with steel, you remove the target, shifting your body or leg out of the line so the attack finds nothing to strike. It may replace a parry entirely or accompany one, and its governing principle is that the good player must void his body whenever he does not strike, so that he is never left standing still in the path of the sword.

Mechanically the void takes several forms. You may carry the left leg crossed behind the right as you deliver a thrust in quarta, swinging your body off the line while your point goes forward. You may void the right foot across, traversing it aside to strike near the adversary's ear. The inquartata is likewise a scanso, a void that carries the body clear of the line at the very moment you drive home a counter-thrust.
records.briefApplication: Void your body whenever you are not striking, so you never remain in the line of the blade; against a wild, over-committed attacker, void backwards to let his blow fall into empty space, then thrust to his face or chest.
records.fullApplication:
Treat the void as your constant companion in defense: any moment you do not answer with a strike of your own, take the body off the line rather than trusting the parry alone. This keeps you safe even when steel does not meet steel.

Against a furious, bestial man who rushes in with reckless force, do not try to stop his blow. Void backwards and let it fall into empty space, spending his commitment on nothing, then answer immediately with a thrust to the face or chest before he can recover.

When you can void and strike in one motion, do so. Carry the left leg crossed behind the right and thrust in quarta, or traverse the right foot aside to strike near the ear, so your body leaves the line in the same tempo your point arrives. The inquartata is the purest expression of this idea, carrying you off the line while your counter-thrust lands.

records.briefDescription: A counter-thrust delivered in quarta while the body voids off the line, the left leg crossing behind the right so that your point reaches the adversary's chest as his attack passes clear.
records.fullDescription:
The inquartata is a counter-thrust thrown in quarta with a void of the body. As you thrust, you carry the left leg crossed behind the right, so that the torso quits the straight line while the adversary's point passes empty and your own point drives to his chest.
