It is most naturally turned against a disengage, or cavazione, or against a pass. You false under the enemy's sword to draw and misdirect his point, then turn the inquartata in quarta and void the body off the line, so that his committed attack finds only empty space where your body stood.

Capo Ferro is openly skeptical of the action in his book on the art, calling the crossing of the left foot worthless and better suited to a friendly assault than to earnest combat; yet he demonstrates the inquartata repeatedly throughout the use.
records.briefApplication: Use it against a disengage or a pass: false under his sword, turn quarta, and void the body with the left leg crossing behind the right so his point passes clear as yours finds his chest.
records.fullApplication:
When the adversary disengages or drives in with a pass, do not meet him by opposing the line but by leaving it. False under his blade to misdirect his point, then turn an inquartata in quarta while the left leg crosses behind the right, carrying your body off the line as your thrust travels to his chest.

The strength of the action is that his committed attack spends itself on the empty line while your point arrives; its weakness, which Capo Ferro himself warns of, is the crossed left foot. Because he judges that crossing worthless and fit more for a friendly assault than for earnest combat, reserve the inquartata for the disengage or pass where the void genuinely clears your body, and do not lean upon it as a staple of earnest play, even though he shows it again and again in the use.

records.briefDescription: A passing thrust to the flank in seconda, made when your constrained adversary disengages at your face: you meet his blade on the outside, pass forward, and strike while seizing his sword hand.
records.fullDescription:
The scannatura is a specific counter used when you already hold the adversary's sword constrained on the outside. Its name comes from scannare, to cut the throat or slaughter, marking it as a killing action rather than a simple defense.

It is formed against his disengage. When he frees his point and thrusts at your face, you meet his sword once more on the outside, lower your point into seconda, and pass with the left leg all in the same tempo. As you pass, you lower the hilt together with the movement of the body so the point drives home, striking him in the flank while your free hand seizes his sword hand. It is therefore a passing thrust to the flank joined to a grip, or grapple, upon his weapon hand.
records.briefApplication: Use it when you have constrained his sword on the outside and he answers with a disengage at your face; meet his blade again outside, drop your point into seconda, and pass in the same tempo to thrust his flank while grasping his sword hand.
records.fullApplication:
The scannatura answers one precise situation. You have constrained his sword on the outside, closing the straight line to him. When he tries to free himself by disengaging and thrusting at your face, do not give ground. In the same tempo, meet his sword again on the outside and lower your point into seconda.

Pass forward with the left leg as you strike, lowering the hilt together with the body so the point enters his flank. With your free hand, seize his sword hand as you thrust. The grip binds his weapon and denies him any means to recover his point, while your passing thrust does its work. Because it is delivered in a single tempo against his disengage, he is left with neither line nor time to answer. The name itself, from scannare, to cut the throat or slaughter, marks it as a killing blow rather than a mere defense.

records.briefDescription: A thrust delivered into the adversary's exposed hand or arm whenever his point strays outside your presence, driven home in mezzo tempo by carrying the body forward along the straight line.
records.fullDescription:
Ferire alla mano is the thrust that answers an uncovered hand. Whenever the adversary carries his point outside your presence, whether high, low, or off to one side, his sword hand is left exposed and becomes the nearest target to strike.

To form it, place the point of your sword directly opposite his hand in a straight line and lean your body somewhat back. Approach to measure, and, having arrived, push a thrust into the hand in mezzo tempo, struck merely by propelling the body forward and bending the right knee while carrying the left foot back accompanied by the right. The same action serves equally against an advanced dagger hand.
records.briefApplication: Use it whenever the adversary's point wanders high, low, or to one side, or when he rushes in without measure or tempo; set your point opposite his hand and thrust into it during his blow.
records.fullApplication:
This is your primary answer to the bestial man who attacks without measure or tempo. Rather than trade blow for blow, strike his sword hand or arm during his blow, meeting his own committed attack in a half tempo instead of opposing it.

Keep your point set opposite his hand in the straight line and lean your body somewhat back, then approach until you arrive at measure. The advanced, uncovered arm is the target of the narrowest measure and of the mezzo tempo, so let his forward commitment carry his hand onto your point. When his point is outside your presence, his hand is the closest and least defended thing to you; thrust into it while carrying the body forward and bending the right knee, drawing the left foot back accompanied by the right as you strike.

records.briefDescription: The core geometric principle of Capo Ferro's method: the single line that divides your body through the flank and joins it to the adversary's, along which the artful seek measure, constrain the sword, and strike.
records.fullDescription:
The straight line is the fundamental geometry on which Capo Ferro builds his entire method. It is the single line that runs from you to the adversary, dividing your body through the flank and joining it to his through the same. Every other path a blade can take is oblique, and the oblique lines are infinite; anyone can make them. The straight line alone is the way of virtue and true reason, and only the artful know how to make it.

Mechanically, to strike in the straight line is to carry your forte before you so that it covers the whole body. When you strike this way in the correct tempo and measure, the adversary can never reach you, with neither thrust nor cut, because your own strong stands between his blade and every opening. The point is held along this line and always aims at the uncovered parts on the adversary's right side.
records.briefApplication: Always seek your measure, constrain the adversary's sword, and deliver along the straight line, keeping your point on the uncovered parts of his right side so your forte covers your whole body as you strike.
records.fullApplication:
Make the straight line the discipline of every action. First seek measure, then constrain the adversary's sword, and only then strike, always along this one line rather than wandering onto the infinite oblique paths that leave you exposed. Because striking straight sets your forte across the whole body, a blow delivered in true tempo and measure cannot be answered: the adversary can hit you with neither thrust nor cut while your strong governs his blade.

Direct your point at the uncovered parts on his right side, where the line finds him open and your cover still holds. Whenever you are tempted toward a wide or crooked blow, remember that anyone can make the oblique lines; the straight line is the mark of the artful, and by holding to it you both defend and offend in a single reasoned motion.

records.briefDescription: The defensive act of turning aside an incoming thrust or cut, made chiefly with the true edge along a straight or oblique line, the point held now high, now low, on an extended arm carried by the feet.
records.fullDescription:
The parata defends the body against an adversary's thrust or cut. You deflect chiefly with the true edge, and only rarely with the falso, tracing either a straight or an oblique line and carrying the point now high, now low according to the attack you must displace.

Its mechanics are exact. Parry with the forte, from the middle of the blade down toward the hilt, using the true edge; when instead you must parry with the falso, oppose the incoming steel from the middle of the blade up toward the point. Every parry demands an extended arm, and it must be carried by the body, the right leg accompanying the defense and the left following after.

Above all it obeys Capo Ferro's governing principle: never parry without answering with a strike. Because he strikes along the straight line, the parry and the strike become a single motion, the forte covering the body in the very moment the thrust goes home.
records.briefApplication: Never parry merely to defend; meet the attacking blade with your forte and true edge and, in the same straight line, drive your own thrust home so that the parry and the strike arrive together.
records.fullApplication:
Because the parry and the strike belong together, defend and offend in one motion. Extend the arm, oppose the adversary's blade with your forte and true edge along the straight line, and let that same action carry your point home. The forte covers your body as the thrust arrives, so that you are never left open in the act of defending. Use the true edge from the middle of the sword down to the hilt for the firmest opposition, reserving the falso, from the middle up to the point, for the rarer occasions that call for it.

When the tempo will not permit a single answer and you must parry in dui tempi, divide the action with the feet. Draw the left foot up to the right as you make the parry, gathering yourself under cover of your forte; then pass forward with the right leg as you deliver the strike. Throughout, keep the arm extended and the point directed as the incoming blow requires, high or low, in a straight or an oblique line, so that hand, blade, and feet move as one.
